goals: Explain the factors responsible for the growth of a composite culture in medieval India
State the main principles of the Bhakti movement
Name some Bhakti saints with their regions and describe their ideas

slides.heading: Composite culture and the Bhakti movement
slides.body_md: Part 1 — why traditions blended, and what the Bhakti saints taught.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the factors behind composite culture, the principles of the Bhakti movement, and the Bhakti saints with their regions
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In medieval India, people of many faiths and languages lived side by side. Over time their ways of life blended into a composite culture. In this part we look at the factors that helped it grow, and then at the Bhakti movement, its principles and its saints.

slides.heading: What is composite culture?
slides.body_md: A shared way of life that grows when different traditions meet.

visual.alt: Flow: many traditions meet, people live and work together, they share language, art and music, and a composite culture grows
visual.caption: How composite culture grows.

slides.narration: A composite culture is a shared way of life formed when people of different traditions meet, live together and mingle their ideas, arts and languages. Nothing is forced on anyone. Each tradition keeps its own character, yet each also borrows from the others, and something new grows.

slides.heading: Six factors behind composite culture
slides.body_md: Several factors worked together.

visual.caption: Six factors behind composite culture.

slides.narration: Look at the web. Six factors helped composite culture grow. People of different faiths lived together for a long time. Rulers gave patronage. The Bhakti and Sufi movements spread love and equality. Trade and towns brought people together. Languages met. And artisans worked for many patrons.

slides.heading: Living together, trade and artisans
bullets: **Long living together**: shared festivals, food and work.
**Trade and towns**: markets brought people into contact.

rows: Neighbours of different faiths shared festivals, food and work
Markets and workshops brought many people into daily contact
Designs and skills passed from one tradition to another

visual.alt: Table of three factors: long living together, with neighbours sharing festivals, food and work; trade and towns, bringing people into daily contact; and artisans working for many patrons, so that designs and skills passed between traditions

slides.narration: When neighbours of different faiths live together for generations, they share festivals, food and work. Trade and towns add to this, because markets and workshops bring many people together every day. Artisans such as carvers and weavers worked for many patrons, so designs and skills passed from one tradition to another.

slides.heading: Patronage by rulers
slides.body_md: Akbar's policy of tolerance is a well known example.

nodes.label: Rulers honour artists, poets and scholars

visual.alt: Flow: rulers honour artists, poets and scholars, different traditions meet at court, and ideas and styles are shared
visual.caption: Patronage by rulers.

slides.narration: Rulers who honoured artists, poets, musicians and scholars gave them a place at court. Artists of different traditions met there and shared ideas and styles. The policy of tolerance followed by the emperor Akbar is a well known example of such patronage.

slides.heading: The meeting of languages
bullets: **Hindavi**, also called **Khari Boli**, was everyday speech of the Delhi region.
**Persian, Arabic and Turkish** words came into it.

rows: Everyday speech of the Delhi region
Many words came into daily speech
Grew from this meeting of languages

visual.alt: Table on the meeting of languages: Hindavi or Khari Boli was everyday speech of the Delhi region, Persian, Arabic and Turkish words came into daily speech, and Urdu grew from the meeting

slides.narration: Languages also met. In the Delhi region people spoke Hindavi, also called Khari Boli. Many Persian, Arabic and Turkish words came into daily speech. Urdu grew from this meeting of languages. Remember that Urdu has roots in the speech of the region itself.

slides.heading: The Bhakti movement
slides.body_md: Devotion and love for a personal God.

rows: Devotion and love for a personal God
Counts for more than elaborate ritual
Teachers and poets from many regions

visual.alt: Table of the meaning of Bhakti: devotion and love for a personal God, sincere devotion counting for more than elaborate ritual, and the saints as teachers and poets from many regions

slides.narration: Bhakti means devotion and love for a personal God. The Bhakti movement was led by saints and poets in many regions. They taught that sincere devotion counts for more than elaborate ritual. In the next slides we look at six principles, three on each slide.

slides.heading: Bhakti principles: devotion, sincerity, the guru
bullets: Devotion and love for **one personal God**.
God reached by **sincere devotion**, not elaborate ritual.

rows: God is reached by sincere devotion, not elaborate ritual

visual.alt: Table of three Bhakti principles: devotion and love for one personal God, sincere devotion rather than elaborate ritual, and the importance of the guru

slides.narration: First, devotion and love for one personal God. Second, God can be reached through sincere devotion rather than elaborate ritual. Third, the guru is important. A teacher guides the devotee on the path of love and right conduct.

slides.heading: Bhakti principles: equality, language, service

rows: Songs and poems in the speech of the people, not only Sanskrit
Devotion shown in conduct towards others

visual.alt: Table of three more Bhakti principles: equality with caste distinctions rejected by many saints, regional languages rather than only Sanskrit, and pure living and service

slides.narration: Fourth, many saints rejected caste distinctions and stressed the equality of all. Fifth, they used regional languages, so ordinary people could understand them, rather than Sanskrit alone. Sixth, they asked for pure living and service. Devotion was shown in how a person treated others.

visual.alt: Table of Bhakti saints of the north: Ramananda of north India, Kabir of Varanasi, Surdas of the Braj region, Tulsidas of the Awadh region who wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, and Mirabai of Rajasthan devoted to Krishna

slides.narration: Ramananda is remembered as a Bhakti teacher of north India. Kabir was a weaver of Varanasi. Surdas was a Bhakti poet of the Braj region. Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a language of the region. Mirabai of Rajasthan is remembered for her devotion to Krishna.

slides.heading: Kabir and Guru Nanak
bullets: **Kabir**: a weaver; **one God** and unity; criticised empty ritual in every faith.
**Guru Nanak** (1469 to 1539): first Sikh Guru; one God, equality, honest work, service, **langar**.

rows: A weaver of Varanasi; one God, unity, and criticism of empty ritual in all faiths
First Sikh Guru, of Punjab; one God, equality, honest work, service and langar

visual.alt: Table of two saints: Kabir, a weaver of Varanasi who stressed one God and unity, and Guru Nanak, 1469 to 1539, the first Sikh Guru of Punjab who stressed one God, equality, honest work, service and langar

slides.narration: Kabir was a weaver of Varanasi. He taught that there is one God, stressed unity among people, and criticised empty ritual in every faith. Guru Nanak, who lived from fourteen sixty nine to fifteen thirty nine, was the first Sikh Guru. He taught one God, equality, honest work and service, and the community meal called langar.

sections.heading: 1. Factors for the growth of a composite culture
sections.body_md:
- **Composite culture:** a shared way of life that grew where different traditions met and mingled.
- **Long living together** of people of different faiths.
- **Patronage by rulers**, for example **Akbar's** policy of tolerance.
- The **Bhakti and Sufi movements**.
- **Trade and towns**.
- **Meeting of languages:** **Urdu** grew from **Hindavi (Khari Boli)** with Persian, Arabic and Turkish words.
- **Artisans** working for many patrons.

key_terms.definition_md: A culture formed by the blending of different traditions.
Everyday speech of the Delhi region, also called Khari Boli.

sections.heading: 2. The Bhakti movement: principles
sections.body_md:
- **Bhakti** means devotion and love for one personal God.
- God can be reached through sincere devotion rather than elaborate ritual.
- Many saints rejected caste distinctions and stressed equality.
- They used regional languages rather than Sanskrit alone.
- The guru is important.
- Pure living and service.

sections.heading: 3. Bhakti saints and their regions
sections.body_md:
- **Ramananda:** north India.
- **Kabir:** a weaver of Varanasi; taught one God and unity and criticised empty ritual in every faith.
- **Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539):** first Sikh Guru; Punjab; taught one God, equality, honest work, service and the community kitchen called **langar**.
- **Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (Bengal and Odisha, about 1486 to 1534):** kirtan.
- **Mirabai:** Rajasthan; devotion to Krishna.
- **Tulsidas:** wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi.
- **Surdas**; **Namdev and Tukaram** (Maharashtra); **Sankardeva** (Assam).
- Earlier south Indian saints: the **Alvars** and **Nayanars**.

sections.heading: 4. The Sufi movement: principles and terms
sections.body_md:
- **Sufis** were mystics within Islam who stressed love and devotion to God, a simple life and service to humanity.
- A spiritual teacher, the **pir** or **sheikh**, guides disciples called **murids**.
- **Khanqahs** (hospices) were open to all.
- **Sama:** devotional music in some orders.
- **Silsilas** (orders): the **Chishti** and the **Suhrawardi** are among the best known in India.

sections.heading: 5. Sufi saints and Amir Khusrau
sections.body_md:
- **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti:** linked with **Ajmer**; died about **1236**.
- **Nizamuddin Auliya:** of **Delhi**; died **1325**.
- **Amir Khusrau (1253 to 1325):** poet and musician; a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya; linked with the **qawwali** tradition and traditionally credited with some musical innovations.
- Shrines of Sufi saints are visited by people of many faiths.

sections.heading: 6. Impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements
sections.body_md:
- **Social harmony** and a message of equality.
- Growth of **regional languages and literature**: Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali, Marathi and others.
- **Devotional music:** kirtan, bhajan, qawwali.
- **Simpler forms of worship.**
- **Shrines and dargahs** visited by people of many faiths.
- **Similarities:** love and devotion, simple life and service, equality, music, local speech.
- **Differences:** guru versus pir and murid; kirtan and bhajan versus sama and qawwali; saints of many regions versus silsilas and khanqahs.

sections.body_md:
- **Architecture:** the Indo-Islamic style joins arches, domes and minarets with brackets, chhatris and carved motifs; **Fatehpur Sikri** is a good example.
- **Music:** Hindustani classical traditions; **Tansen** at Akbar's court.
- **Painting:** Mughal miniatures blended Persian and Indian styles.
- **Language and literature:** Urdu; Persian translations of Sanskrit works.
- **Missionaries:** Portuguese reach India 1498 (Vasco da Gama); **St Francis Xavier** at Goa 1542; a printing press at Goa about 1556; Jesuits at Akbar's court about 1580; **William Carey** at Serampore from 1800, with presses and translations including into Bengali.
- They founded **schools and colleges, hospitals and orphanages**, and some opposed social evils.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up the saints and their regions, or giving a saint without a region.
- Writing that Amir Khusrau was a disciple of Moinuddin Chishti (he was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya).
- Writing that Urdu has no link with the speech of the region.
- Ranking one faith or saint above another, or using unkind words.
- Quoting verses instead of paraphrasing the ideas.
- Writing about the missionaries beyond education and social service.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: Ms Devika, an imagined language teacher in Lakshmipur, tells her class that in the Delhi region everyday Hindavi speech took in many Persian, Arabic and Turkish words, and that Urdu grew in this way. Which factor of composite culture does she describe?

options.text_md: The end of all trade between towns
The meeting of languages through daily contact
The ban on every regional speech
The rule that only one language could be written

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The meeting of languages through daily contact. Urdu grew as words of several languages mixed in everyday speech, a meeting of languages. Trade did not end, regional speech was not banned, and many languages were in use.

questions.stem_md: A plaque at the imagined Heritage Club of Navnagar says that a ruler welcomed poets, singers and scholars of different faiths at his court and gave them gifts and honour. Which factor of composite culture does the plaque best illustrate?

options.text_md: The complete separation of every community
The closing of all temples, mosques and markets
A law that all artists must follow one tradition
Patronage by rulers, as in the policy of tolerance followed by Akbar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Patronage by rulers, as in the policy of tolerance followed by Akbar. Rulers who honoured artists and scholars of many faiths show patronage, which Akbar's tolerance is a good example of. The other options describe separation or compulsion, which do not build a blended culture.

questions.stem_md: On the imagined heritage walk of Class IX-B through the old bazaar of Kamalpur, the guide points out a lane where a cloth merchant, a dyer and a bangle-maker of different faiths run shops side by side. Which factor of composite culture does the lane show?

options.text_md: Trade and towns, which brought different people into daily contact
The fall of all towns and the closing of markets
A rule that each faith must trade in a separate town

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Trade and towns, which brought different people into daily contact. A busy bazaar where people of different faiths work together is the effect of trade and towns. The other options describe the opposite: no towns, forced separation or no crafts.

questions.stem_md: Ghulam, an imagined stone-carver of Shilpapur, has carved a window screen for a temple, a pattern for a mosque and a balcony for a merchant's house in the same season. What does this show about medieval India?

options.text_md: Each artisan could work only for one faith
Artisans worked for many patrons and their skills were shared across traditions
Artisans had no skills worth sharing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Artisans worked for many patrons and their skills were shared across traditions. One craftsman serving different patrons shows artisans working for many patrons, so skills and designs crossed between traditions. The other options deny this evidence.

questions.stem_md: The imagined school magazine of Madhavpur explains composite culture to Class IX readers. Which explanation is correct?

options.text_md: A culture in which one tradition forced all others to disappear
A culture that grew in one town and never spread
A shared way of life formed when people of different traditions lived together and mingled ideas, arts and languages
A culture made only of royal court ceremonies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A shared way of life formed when people of different traditions lived together and mingled ideas, arts and languages. Composite culture means a blend that grew out of contact between traditions. It was not forced on others, was not limited to one town and was not only a court ceremony.

questions.stem_md: A group project in the imagined Kaveripur History Club lists factors for the growth of composite culture in medieval India. Which entry does NOT belong on the list?

options.text_md: A rule that no two communities may meet or trade
Long living together of people of different faiths

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A rule that no two communities may meet or trade. A rule keeping communities apart would block blending, so it is not a factor. Living together, artisans serving many patrons and the Bhakti and Sufi movements all helped composite culture grow.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Urdu is often given as an example of the meeting of languages in medieval India.

**Reason (R):** Urdu grew from Hindavi, also called Khari Boli, as many Persian, Arabic and Turkish words were taken into it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. The way Urdu grew by taking words from several languages into a language of the region is exactly what makes it an example of languages meeting.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Patronage by rulers helped composite culture to grow.

**Reason (R):** Rulers who gave gifts and honour to artists and scholars of different traditions brought them together at court, where they shared ideas.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Court patronage placed artists of different traditions side by side, so ideas, styles and skills were shared, which explains how patronage helped composite culture.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A visitor to the imagined museum at Sundarnagar says that Urdu grew only from Persian, with no link to the speech of the people of the region.
questions.solution_md: **False.** Urdu grew from Hindavi (Khari Boli), a language of the region, with Persian, Arabic and Turkish words added.

questions.stem_md: Savitri, an imagined villager of Gopalpur, says that she cannot afford grand ceremonies but believes that sincere devotion to the one God she loves is enough. Which principle of the Bhakti movement does her belief match?

options.text_md: God can be reached only by costly ceremonies
God can be reached only by the rich
God cannot be reached at all
God can be reached through sincere devotion rather than elaborate ritual

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** God can be reached through sincere devotion rather than elaborate ritual. Bhakti saints taught that loving, sincere devotion mattered more than elaborate ritual. The other options say the reverse or deny that God can be reached.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined evening gathering of devotees in Bhaktipur, a weaver, a potter and a farmer sit in one row and sing together, and nobody is asked about birth or caste. Which Bhakti principle does this scene show?

options.text_md: The rule that each caste must sing separately
Rejection of caste distinctions and the equality of all in devotion
The rule that only priests may sing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rejection of caste distinctions and the equality of all in devotion. Many Bhakti saints rejected caste distinctions and stressed equality. The other options describe separation, a priestly monopoly or a ban, which Bhakti did not teach.

questions.stem_md: A notebook of the imagined music teacher Mr Rao at Pandharpur records that the saint-poets of the region composed their songs in the Marathi spoken by farmers and traders, not in Sanskrit. Which Bhakti principle does this show?

options.text_md: Use of regional languages rather than Sanskrit
A rule that songs must be written only in Persian
The belief that only Sanskrit scholars may pray

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Use of regional languages rather than Sanskrit. Bhakti saints used the regional languages of ordinary people. They did not restrict worship to Sanskrit or Persian, and they did not ban songs.

questions.stem_md: Tara, an imagined disciple in a village near Varanasi, walks each morning to her teacher, who guides her in prayer and in right conduct. Which principle of the Bhakti movement does this illustrate?

options.text_md: The rule that no one needs guidance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The importance of the guru. Bhakti stressed the importance of the guru as a guide on the path of devotion. The other options contradict this.

questions.stem_md: A label in the imagined Weavers' Gallery at Kashipur describes a weaver of Varanasi who taught that there is one God, stressed unity among people and criticised empty ritual in every faith. Which Bhakti saint does it describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Kabir. The weaver of Varanasi who stressed one God and unity is Kabir. Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas, Mirabai is linked with Rajasthan, and Chaitanya with Bengal and Odisha.

questions.stem_md: A quiz card at the imagined Punjab Study Camp reads: born in 1469, the first Guru of the Sikhs, taught one God, equality, honest work and service, and the community kitchen called langar. Whose name belongs on the card?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Guru Nanak. Guru Nanak (1469 to 1539) was the first Sikh Guru, from Punjab. Sankardeva is linked with Assam, Tukaram with Maharashtra and Surdas with devotion to Krishna.

questions.stem_md: The imagined librarian of Ayodhya Road School shows a catalogue card for the Ramcharitmanas by Tulsidas and asks in which language it was written. What is the correct answer?

(ii) Saints composed in the speech of the people, so **Hindi, Punjabi, Bengali, Marathi** and other languages gained rich literature, and ordinary people could read and hear devotional writing in their own speech, which enriched the languages themselves.

(iii) **Kirtan, bhajan and qawwali** developed as devotional music. Worship became **simpler**, with less stress on elaborate ceremony, and **shrines and dargahs** were visited by people of many faiths, becoming places of peace and shared respect.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In **1498** the Portuguese reached India under **Vasco da Gama**. **St Francis Xavier** came to **Goa** in **1542**, and about **1556** a **printing press** was set up in Goa, an early press in India.
